fixed_reference.title: Gate 0 · fixed expressions
fixed_reference.note: Checked automatically before any question is asked. Set phrases override every rule below, so they get caught first. Each one carries the section it comes from.

determiners.explanation: The slot before the noun is already filled. English allows only one determiner there, so an article is neither needed nor possible: my book, never the my book. This is not a zero-article rule — the question simply does not arise.
determiners.possessive_s_note: A possessive 's fills the same slot: Sarah's car.

constructions.name: there_is_singular
constructions.explanation: There is / there are in the 'something exists' sense introduces something the listener does not yet know about, so a singular noun takes a/an.
examples: There's a post office in my town.
constructions.contrast: An uncountable noun after there is takes no article instead: There is always traffic on this road. And there can mean 'in a certain place', where no special rule applies: There are the books that I lost!

constructions.name: there_are_plural
constructions.explanation: There are in the 'something exists' sense takes a plural noun, and it is normal to use a number or no article rather than an article.
examples: There are two train stations in Glasgow.
There are butterflies in my garden.
There is always traffic on this road.
constructions.contrast: There meaning 'in a certain place' is different: There are the books that I lost!

constructions.name: exclamation_what_a
constructions.explanation: An exclamation with what and a singular countable noun takes a/an.

constructions.name: exclamation_what
constructions.article: a / an with a singular countable noun, otherwise no article
constructions.explanation: An exclamation with what takes a/an before a singular countable noun, and no article before a plural or uncountable one.

constructions.name: unique_role
constructions.explanation: A job that is the only one of its kind in an organisation takes no article after verbs such as elect, appoint, become and be, or after as.
examples: Julie was appointed headteacher of our school.
Luke started working as CEO last week.
constructions.contrast: An ordinary job takes a/an, and a role identified for the listener takes the: Julie is a headteacher, Julie is the headteacher of our school. (5.2)

constructions.name: in_the_next_last
constructions.explanation: In the next / last + a time word takes the, and means a stretch running from now: in the next year is 'between now and a year from now', which is different from next year.
examples: I'll finish my thesis in the next year.
I lost my credit card sometime in the last week.

constructions.name: next_last_time
constructions.explanation: With next time and last time either the or no article works.
examples: (The) next time we go out, I'll bring my umbrella.
(The) last time I saw her, she looked really tired.

constructions.name: next_last_time_word
constructions.explanation: Next and last with a time expression take no article, even though they usually take the as adjectives (2.4.4).
examples: I'm going to visit my brother next week.
I went on holiday to Bolivia last summer.
constructions.contrast: With an ordinary noun they do take the: We'll get on the next bus, He ate the last chocolate.

constructions.name: ordinal_prize
constructions.explanation: First prize and second place in races and competitions are fixed expressions and take no article.

constructions.name: ordering_ideas
constructions.explanation: Used alone to put ideas in order, an ordinal takes no article.
examples: First, you mix the flour. Second, you add the water.

constructions.name: a_ordinal_one_more
constructions.explanation: A/an with an ordinal means 'one more', not 'the Nth one in a row'. Less common than the.
examples: Would you like a second cup of coffee?
We missed two buses, but thankfully a third bus came along.

constructions.name: next_last_adjective
constructions.explanation: As ordinary adjectives, next and last take the, because they identify which one you mean.
examples: We'll get on the next bus.
I can't believe he ate the last chocolate!
constructions.contrast: With a time expression they take no article instead: next week, last summer. (7.11)

constructions.name: ordinal_noun
constructions.explanation: An ordinal takes the when it makes clear which one you mean.
examples: She bought the first dress she found.
I'd like the third cake on the shelf.
constructions.contrast: A/an is possible when it does not identify which one, meaning 'one more': Would you like a second cup of coffee?

constructions.name: comparative_pair
constructions.explanation: The the + comparative, the + comparative structure says that two things change together. Both halves take the.
examples: The sunnier it is, the happier I am.
The more work you do, the better your result will be.
The hotter the curry, the better!

constructions.name: the_most
constructions.explanation: The most is part of a superlative with a long adjective, and implies a comparison (2.4.5). With a noun it means 'the largest number of'.
examples: Lucy is the most intelligent student in the class.
James has the most books of the people in the class.

constructions.name: most_of_the
constructions.explanation: Most itself takes no article. Most of the + noun keeps the same meaning as bare most, and needs the because that noun is specific.
examples: Most of the people in the class like cake.
Most of the cats in London wear collars.

constructions.name: most_noun
constructions.explanation: Most before a noun means 'almost all' or 'very many', and takes no article.

constructions.name: bare_few_little
constructions.explanation: Bare few and little take no article and mean 'almost none' - noticeably less than a few and a little, which mean 'a small amount, but enough'.
examples: Sorry, I have little money. I really can't afford to go out.
There have been few problems with the new system, thankfully!
constructions.contrast: Compare I have a little money, enough for the cinema with I have little money. With something unwanted, the bare form is positive: there is little crime in my town.

constructions.name: one_of_the
constructions.explanation: Use one, not a/an, before of the, of these or of those.
examples: One of the students cheated in the exam.
I think Madonna lives in one of these houses.

constructions.name: a_with_large_numbers
constructions.explanation: A/an is the normal choice before hundred, thousand, million and fractions like third and quarter. One is possible but emphasises the number.
examples: My great-aunt is a hundred years old.
About a quarter of the earth's surface is covered by land.

constructions.name: and_a_half
constructions.explanation: After a number, half takes a: two and a half hours. The same applies after a word saying how much or how long, and that word must also take a.
examples: It took two and a half hours to get to the airport.
We were in Paris for a week and a half.

constructions.name: half_zero
constructions.explanation: Half normally takes no article of its own, and one is not used with it.
examples: Could I have half of the pizza, please?
We walked along the beach for about half an hour.

constructions.name: body_part_after_verb
constructions.explanation: After certain verbs - touch, shoot, take, pull, hit, kick, pat, grab, hold, kiss - a part of the body takes the after a preposition. It is almost a fixed phrase.
examples: She touched him on the arm.
The criminal shot the policeman in the leg.
constructions.contrast: Normally a body part takes a possessive instead: I've hurt my leg, He broke his arm.

constructions.name: family_surname
constructions.explanation: The + surname + s means that family.
examples: The Smiths are coming to dinner.
We've been invited on holiday with the Blacks.

constructions.name: unknown_person
constructions.explanation: A/an before a name says you do not know the person, or are uncertain who they are.
examples: A Mr Thompson called for you.
There's a Jane Green at the door.

constructions.name: titled_name
constructions.explanation: People's names take no article, including a title used with the name, and family words like Mum and Grandpa.
examples: Aunt Mary and Uncle David have invited us to lunch.

languages.explanation:
Languages take no article: She speaks Japanese, They're studying Spanish.

Note that the word language itself is an ordinary noun: the language I speak at home, a new language.
languages.unusual: If the word is used in an unusual way it stops being an exception and the ordinary rules apply again: the French that they speak in Montreal, a beautiful Spanish, the football they play in the USA. (6.1.4)

meals.explanation: Meals take no article: What shall we have for dinner?, I didn't eat breakfast.
meals.unusual: A special occasion, or an adjective before the meal, brings the article back: The lunch we had after the wedding, There will be a dinner for her birthday, an early supper. (6.1.4)

sports.explanation: Sports and games take no article: I don't like golf, He often plays tennis, John loves playing rugby.
sports.unusual: If the word is used in an unusual way it stops being an exception and the ordinary rules apply again: the French that they speak in Montreal, a beautiful Spanish, the football they play in the USA. (6.1.4)

time_words.unusual: A time word used in an unusual way - a particular one you both know - takes the: Do you remember the Monday we met?, The June when we got married. And a with a day means 'any': Could we meet on a Monday? (6.2.8)

months.explanation: Months take no article. The tense of the sentence says which one you mean: I'll see you in December (next), We met in December (last).

days.explanation: Days of the week take no article: I'm meeting Julia on Monday, She started work last Wednesday. A plural day means 'every': I work on Mondays and Tuesdays.

holidays.explanation: Holidays and special days take no article: on Christmas Day, during Ramadan, at Halloween.

seasons.explanation:
Seasons take either the or no article: She goes to Spain in summer, I don't go to the park in the winter, Autumn is my favourite season.

With fall (US English) the is the more common choice.

periods.explanation: Historical periods take the: during the Renaissance, in the Middle Ages.

year.explanation: Years take no article: She was born in 1991, This castle was built in 1672.

decade.explanation: Decades take the: The Beatles were popular in the 1960s, I became interested in music in the eighties.

century.explanation: Centuries take the: Shakespeare was born in the sixteenth century.

date_number_first.explanation: A date with the number first takes the (most common in British English): We got married on the 22nd of September.

date_number_second.explanation: A date with the number second takes no article (most common in US English): She met him on November 16th.

day_part.explanation:
A part of the day takes no article when you name the day with it: On Wednesday night we went to the theatre, I met John on Friday morning.

On its own it is different: in the morning, at night (4.12).

proper_noun_the.explanation: Plural names, of-constructions, rivers, seas, oceans, deserts, mountain ranges, regions, hotels, museums, theatres and newspapers take the. This is a closed list — learn it as one group.
proper_noun_the.matching_note: A keyword only counts inside a capitalised name (the Nile River, not a storm crossed the desert), and an of-construction needs a capitalised word on each side (the Republic of Ireland, not a cup of coffee).

nationality_the.explanation: Nationality adjectives ending in -ish, -ch or -ese take the when they mean the people of that country as a whole: the British, the French. The plural noun form takes no article: Germans, Kenyans.

phonetics.note: A or an is chosen by the sound the next word starts with, not by the letter.

vowel_letter_consonant_sound.why: Starts with a vowel letter but a consonant sound: a university, a European, a one-way street.

consonant_letter_vowel_sound.why: A silent h leaves a vowel sound: an hour, an honest answer.

initialisms.why: An initialism is read letter by letter, so the letter's own name decides: an MBA (em), an FBI agent (ef), a UFO (you).

word_acronyms.why: An acronym pronounced as a word follows the word's sound, not its letters: a NASA engineer.

noun_number.explanation: When a noun is followed by a classifying number or letter — Page 42, Platform 9, Question B — English uses no article. The number does the identifying that the would otherwise do.

noun_adjunct.explanation: In a noun-noun pair the first noun works like an adjective, so the article is decided entirely by the second noun.

determiner_conflict.explanation: This noun has a fixed sense, but the article already in your sentence points at a different one. The fixed rule does not apply here.

q2.q: Is it a proper noun — a name?
q2.note: A name picks out one particular person, place, day, language or brand — and it is written with a capital letter.

opts.label: Yes — a name
opts.ex: Sarah · Madrid · Everest · Monday · Spanish · Toyota

opts.label: No — a kind of thing
opts.ex: friend · city · mountain · day · language · car

q2a.q: Is it in the the-taking class of names?
q2a.note: Plural names, of-constructions, water and landforms, regions, buildings and publications.

opts.label: Yes
opts.ex: the Netherlands · the Alps · the Republic of Ireland · the Nile · the Mediterranean · the Sahara · the Middle East · the Prado · the Guardian

opts.label: No
opts.ex: Madrid · Spain · Micah · Everest · Portuguese · President Sánchez

outPropThe.cat: Question 2a · name in the the-taking class
outPropThe.why: Plural names, of-constructions, rivers, seas, oceans, deserts, mountain ranges, regions, hotels, museums, theaters and newspapers take the. This is a closed list — learn it as one.

outPropZero.why: People, cities, single countries, single mountains, streets, continents, languages and companies take no article. Also titles used with a name: President Sánchez, Doctor Ruiz — but the president on its own is a role noun and routes to 4g.

q3.q: Am I talking about the whole class, or about particular instances?
q3.note: Test: can you insert in general without changing the meaning? If yes, it's generic.

opts.label: The class as a whole — generic
opts.ex: Dogs, <ins>in general</ins>, are loyal. · Life, <ins>in general</ins>, is hard.

opts.label: Particular instances
opts.ex: I saw a dog. · The dog bit me.

q3.warn: Highest-error node for a Spanish speaker. La vida es dura becomes Life is hard, not the life. When you're unsure at this question, generic plus zero is the safer guess.

q3a.q: How is the noun behaving here?
q3a.note: All three forms can be generic in English. This is the one place where the and a and zero are all live options for the same meaning.

opts.label: Plural countable
opts.ex: Dogs are loyal.

opts.label: Non-count or abstract
opts.ex: Life is hard. · She studies economics.

opts.label: Singular countable, any representative
opts.ex: A dog needs exercise.

opts.label: Singular countable, the species
opts.ex: The dog is a social animal.

outGenZeroPl.why: The default way to talk about a whole class in English. Reach for this first when the generic reading is what you want.

outGenZeroNc.why:
Abstractions and mass nouns take no article in their generic sense: water, life, music, economics, happiness, advice. This is the single biggest source of article errors for Romance-language speakers.

One exception worth knowing: in formal or literary English you can put a/an on an uncountable noun when you name a particular type of it, almost always with an adjective — a profound sadness, an excellent knowledge of history. (7.2)

outGenA.why: Picks out any arbitrary member to stand for the class. Slightly more formal than the plural, and it won't work with every predicate — A dog is widespread fails, because being widespread is true of the species and not of any individual.

outGenThe.why: Names the class as a single entity. Formal and mostly scientific: The blue whale is endangered. It does not work with every predicate — The tiger is endangered is fine, The tiger is everywhere is not. Note this reading is only reachable from Question 3.

q4.q: Can my listener identify which one I mean?
q4.note: Take the first option only if nothing below fits. Otherwise work down the list — the first match is your answer, and the labels just tell you why.
q4.group: Everything below answers the — pick the first one that matches

opts.label: 4a · The sentence itself specifies it
opts.ex: the book I lent you · the man in the corner · the capital of Spain

opts.label: 4b · There's a superlative, ordinal or uniqueness word
opts.ex: the best · the first · the only · the same · the next

opts.label: 4c · We've mentioned it already
opts.ex: I bought a car. The car was red.

opts.label: 4d · It's inferable from something we mentioned
opts.ex: I bought a car. The engine was noisy.

opts.label: 4e · There's only one in the world
opts.ex: the sun · the equator · the internet

opts.label: 4f · There's only one in our shared community
opts.ex: the mall · the beach · the park · the gym · the doctor

opts.label: 4g · It's a role that belongs to something
opts.ex: the government · the president · the economy · the weather

opts.label: None of these — my listener can't tell which one

out4a.why:
A relative clause (2.4.1), a prepositional phrase (2.4.2) or an of-phrase (2.4.3) narrows the noun to one referent, so the identification happens inside the sentence itself.

Careful: a modifier alone is not enough. It has to make the referent identifiable. I met a woman who speaks Icelandic keeps a, because the clause describes her rather than picking out which woman is meant.

out4b.why: Best, first, only, same, next, last, main all entail that there's exactly one, so the follows automatically.

out4c.why: The classic a → the switch. First mention introduces, second mention points back.

out4d.why: Part-whole and possession relations license this without any prior mention of the noun itself. A car has one engine, a room has one ceiling, so naming the whole makes the part identifiable.

out4e.why: Shared world knowledge does the identifying. No context needed at all.

q4f.q: Does the noun name a place, or an institutional activity?
q4f.note: This is where the mall and at school collide. Both are familiar community places, so the wrong branch is easy to take.

opts.label: A place
opts.ex: mall · beach · park · gym · bank · airport · library · store

opts.label: An institutional activity or state
opts.ex: school · church · class · prison · court · bed · work · sea

q4f.warn: Compare at school, meaning studying, with at the school, meaning standing in the building. The activity set is closed and somewhat arbitrary — I'm at school is available but I'm at library isn't.

out4f.cat: 4f · only one in our shared community
out4f.why: No specific one has been mentioned, and none needs to be. I'm at the mall doesn't identify which mall — it relies on your listener not needing to ask. This still holds for a mall neither of you has ever visited, because what's required is that the question which one? doesn't arise, not that a particular referent exists.

outActivityZero.why:
When the noun names the activity an institution exists for rather than its building, English drops the article: at school (studying), in prison (serving a sentence), in bed (sleeping), at work (working), in class, at sea, in court.

Put the back the moment you mean the building instead: I parked at the school.

out4g.cat: 4g · a role that belongs to something
out4g.why: Role nouns are inherently of something: government of a country, capital of a country, manager of a team. The article is licensed because the noun carries an implicit slot that context fills — and the slot can stay unfilled out loud. What should the government do? works between an American and a Spaniard discussing neither country, because it means the government of whatever situation we're discussing. Unique relative to an argument, not unique in the world.

q5.q: How am I using the noun here — countable or not?
q5.note: Ask about this use, not about the noun. Coffee and a coffee. Experience and an experience. Paper and a paper. A noun-property question sends dual-membership nouns down the wrong branch and keeps them there.

opts.label: Singular countable
opts.ex: I saw a dog. · She's a teacher. · I need a pen.

opts.label: Plural countable
opts.ex: I bought books.

opts.label: Non-count
opts.ex: We need water.

out5a.why: Countable, singular, and your listener can't yet tell which one. Covers first mention, non-specific any uses, and classifying after be — She is a doctor (5.2).

out5zPl.why: The plural counterpart of a. English has no plural indefinite article, so the slot stays empty. Add some if you need to signal quantity (Appendix 3).

out5zNc.why: Mass nouns take no article when indefinite. Add a quantifier if you need one: some water, a lot of water.

traces.p: There's a post office in my town
